title: On top of Everest, water boils at about 71 °C
body: Water boils when the pressure of its own vapour matches the pressure of the air pressing down on it. At sea level that takes 100 °C, but on Everest’s summit, 8,849 m up, the air pushes with only about **a third of the force**, roughly 34 kPa, so water boils at about 71 °C. Climbers’ tea is lukewarm, and a boiled egg stays runny, because the water simply cannot get any hotter than that without a pressure cooker.

slides.question: How much of sea-level air pressure is left on Everest’s summit?
slides.explanation: About 34 kPa against 101 kPa at sea level: roughly a third. That is why water boils so cool up there.

slides.heading: On Everest’s summit, only about a third of sea-level air pressure is left
slides.note: About 34 kPa against 101 kPa at sea level, so water boils at about 71 °C

slides.alt: A mountain outline with four marked heights: sea level 100 °C, 1,500 m 95 °C, 4,500 m about 85 °C, and the 8,849 m summit about 71 °C.
slides.caption: Lower air pressure, lower boiling point.

slides.label: air pressure on the summit, about a third of the 101 kPa at sea level
slides.text: With less air pushing down, water molecules escape as vapour at a lower temperature. Boiling is the vapour winning that contest.

slides.heading: Why food cooks slowly
slides.text: Cooking speed depends on temperature, not on bubbling. At 71 °C, pasta, rice and eggs cook far slower, and some things never soften. Darwin complained that in the high Andes, potatoes left in boiling water for hours were still almost as hard as ever.

slides.heading: The fix
slides.text: A pressure cooker seals the steam in, raising the pressure and with it the boiling point, which is why high-altitude kitchens rely on them. The opposite trick works too: in a vacuum chamber, water boils at room temperature.

slides.heading: Where does water boil?
slides.explanation: Boiling point rises and falls with the pressure on the water: a sealed pressure cooker raises it, thin mountain air or a vacuum lowers it.
